section_summary: This section covers State Department records from March to July 1939 detailing Japan's internal political reorganization, wartime economic mobilization, and foreign policy during the Sino-Japanese conflict. Documents include diplomatic despatches, telegrams, and Far Eastern Affairs division memoranda analyzing the implementation of the National General Mobilization Law, the 1939 Commodity Mobilization Plan, the National Spiritual Mobilization Movement, and the drive toward Yen Bloc autarchy. Diplomatic reporting focuses on Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's farewell conversations with Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita concerning Japan's position between the Axis and the democracies, alongside army dominance over continental administration through the Asia Promotion Board.

subfiles.about: Comprehensive consular report examining Japanese public sentiment toward foreign powers, the Three Year Production Expansion Plan, and acute domestic economic and financial strains.
subfiles.summary: This concluding segment of a voluntary consular report analyzes Japanese official policy toward Jewish refugees and local public attitudes in the Kansai region toward the United States, Great Britain, and France. It underscores Japan's vital dependence on American imports of petroleum, scrap iron, machine tools, and technology, contrasting this with rising resentment toward British and French assistance to China. The report outlines the government's Three Year Production Expansion Plan and National General Mobilization Law designed to enforce Yen Bloc autarchy. Finally, it surveys severe financial and industrial stresses, including dwindling gold reserves, raw material shortages, mandatory rationing of fuel and metals, inflation, and weakening domestic capacity to absorb war bonds.
subfiles.title: Report on Japanese Economic Mobilization, Foreign Relations, and Strained Financial Situation
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3815 regarding new cabinet appointments for Overseas Affairs and Communications.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Salisbury reviews Despatch 3815: Koiso's Overseas Affairs appointment placated nationalist reformers, Tanabe gave Hiranuma a loyalist, praising Schuler's despatch for showing how the appointments reinforced the cabinet.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3815 Regarding Cabinet Appointments
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting and analyzing the appointments of General Kuniaki Koiso as Minister for Overseas Affairs and Harumichi Tanabe as Minister of Communications.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the official gazetting of General Kuniaki Koiso as Minister for Overseas Affairs and Harumichi Tanabe as Minister of Communications, ending the concurrent holding of these posts by other ministers. The despatch reviews Koiso's career in Manchuria and Korea, his connections with nationalist bodies such as the Kokuhonsha, and his role in continental emigration. It also evaluates Tanabe's administrative career in communications and close alignment with Premier Hiranuma, concluding that the appointments were designed to relieve overburdened ministers, appease right-wing critics, and improve cabinet efficiency.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3815: Appointment of Full-Time Minister for Overseas Affairs and Minister of Communications

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Telegram No. 205 concerning Prime Minister Hiranuma's political commitments and cabinet instability.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Tokyo telegram reports Hiranuma compromised with nationalist groups planning to abolish the Diet for direct Imperial rule.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Tokyo Telegram No. 205 Concerning Cabinet Security and Imperial Temporal Power

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Paris Telegram No. 557 concerning Japanese militarist efforts to oust Foreign Minister Arita and secure an Axis military alliance.
subfiles.from: William C. Bullitt, American Ambassador to France, Paris
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Paris telegram relays French intelligence that Japanese militarists sought to overthrow Arita for a German-Italian alliance.
subfiles.title: Document File Note on Paris Telegram No. 557 Concerning Japanese Militarists and Axis Alliance

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Tokyo Telegram No. 235 concerning Foreign Minister Arita's positions on European alignments and American rights in China.
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Ballantine reviews Grew's farewell talk with Arita, warning an Anglo-French-Soviet alliance could push Japan toward the Axis, noting conditional U.S.-commerce/Settlement assurances amid Japan's incompatible 'New Order in East Asia' doctrine.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Telegram No. 235 Regarding Conversation with Foreign Minister Arita
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Six-section telegram reporting Ambassador Grew's extensive farewell interview with Foreign Minister Arita on Axis negotiations, European war, China policy, and South Seas security.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew transmits a detailed account in six sections of his farewell conference with Foreign Minister Hachiro Arita prior to taking home leave. Arita assured Grew that negotiations with Germany and Italy were strictly confined to anti-Comintern measures rather than a general military alliance, though he warned that a British-French-Soviet pact would force Japan to reconsider its position. Arita maintained that interferences with American commerce in China were temporary military necessities and denied intentions to seize the International Settlements in Shanghai or Kulangsu. Additionally, Arita delivered confidential oral statements defending Japan's 'New Order in East Asia' and offering bilateral discussions to dispel American apprehensions regarding Japanese territorial ambitions in the South Seas and the Philippines following the occupation of Hainan Island and the Spratly Islands.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 235 from Tokyo: Farewell Interview with Foreign Minister Arita on Foreign Policy and the New Order

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3905 concerning the Japanese government's National Spiritual Mobilization Movement.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Despatch 3905 on April 1939 spiritual-mobilization programs eliminating Kuomintang influence and third-power interference, enforcing austerity and savings, though stopping short of gold confiscation or capital levies.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3905 Regarding National Spiritual Mobilization
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the reorganization, objectives, and concrete methods of the National Spiritual Mobilization Movement in Japan.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d'Affaires a.i., American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Dooman reports on the reorganization of the National Spiritual Mobilization Movement through the creation of a ministerial liaison committee and the adoption of foundational programs in April 1939. The despatch details eight specific methods promulgated to discipline civilian life, including simplified living, commodity conservation, waste reclamation, gold acquisition, and a Yen 10,000,000,000 national savings drive. Dooman examines the growth of state-directed social controls under the National General Mobilization Law, concluding that while moral exhortation remains prominent, administrative compulsion and intimidation are steadily increasing.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3905: The National Spiritual Mobilization Movement

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3955 concerning the adoption of the 1939 Commodity Mobilization Plan.
subfiles.summary: Memo outlines Despatch 3955 on the secret May 1939 Commodity Mobilization Plan, shifting from voluntary compliance to state compulsion favoring munitions/export production, with rationing, coupons, and resource transfers to Manchukuo/North China.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3955 Regarding Commodity Mobilization Plans
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Comprehensive despatch analyzing the secret adoption and seven major components of the Japanese government's 1939 Commodity Mobilization Plan.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d'Affaires a.i., American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Dooman analyzes the 1939 Commodity Mobilization Plan drafted by the Cabinet Planning Board under Kazuo Aoki and approved in late May under strict official secrecy. The report details seven operational provisions: expansion of strategic productive capacity, export promotion to secure foreign exchange, industrial resource transfers to Manchukuo and North China, curtailment of daily necessities, six-tier prioritized distribution, consumption regulation through coupon rationing, and coordination of communications and electric power. Dooman concludes that Japan's economy has entered a decisive stage of compulsory state control, establishing a regimented socialist war economy under the National General Mobilization Law.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3955: Plans for Commodity Mobilization

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 3983 on Japan's accelerating drive toward autarchy under the National Mobilization Law.
subfiles.summary: Memo summarizes Japan's self-sufficiency drive under the 1938 Mobilization Law: restricted export-goods consumption, substitute-material research, falling living standards, and public adaptation via imperial 'kinnoron' spirit easing the shift to state autarchy.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 3983 Regarding National Mobilization and Autarchy
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Detailed despatch examining the rapid invocation of the National General Mobilization Law and Japan's systematic transition to economic autarchy.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Chargé d'Affaires a.i., American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: Dooman reviews the implementation of the National General Mobilization Law, reporting that 14 of 23 prepared articles have been promulgated to meet mainland military requirements and counter domestic inflation. The despatch examines intense industrial efforts to develop domestic substitutes for imported materials such as wool, cotton, petroleum, and non-ferrous metals, alongside the creation of a Foreign Trade Council. Dooman observes that traditional social deference and an intense spiritual devotion to the Emperor ('kinnoron') are enabling the Japanese public to accept declining living standards and regimented state control without popular revolt.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 3983: National Mobilization and the Development of Autarchy in Japan

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Peiping Despatch No. 2079 regarding bureaucratic rivalries and military control in the Asia Promotion Board.
subfiles.summary: Memo reviews Peiping's report that Asia Promotion Board liaison offices function poorly amid military-civil-commercial division, concluding Itagaki and the army aim to displace civilians and secure exclusive continental control.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Peiping Despatch No. 2079 Regarding the Asia Promotion Board
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on inter-agency discord, lack of esprit de corps, and military dominance within the Peking Liaison Office of the Asia Promotion Board.
subfiles.from: Frank P. Lockhart, Counselor of Embassy, Peiping
subfiles.summary: Lockhart reports the Peking Liaison Office riven by Army/Navy/civilian/commercial factionalism with military vetoes, concluding Itagaki's army leadership uses the Board to strip Foreign Office authority and exclude civilians permanently.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2079: The Peking Liaison Office of the Asia Promotion Board

subfiles.about: Routing memorandum by Adviser on Political Relations Hornbeck commending an attached Tokyo despatch on Japanese public psychology drafted by Cabot Coville.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck routes Despatch 4000 to Hamilton, Welles, and Hull, praising it as exceptionally well-written, crediting junior officer Coville's psychological analysis of Japanese social classes.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Adviser on Political Relations Hornbeck Commending Tokyo Despatch No. 4000 on Japanese War Psychology
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Sumner Welles, and Cordell Hull

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 4000 regarding public psychology, wartime economic boom conditions, and social attitudes in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Memo summarizes Despatch 4000 on wartime Japanese morale: public reconciled via war-boom wages, while the squeezed middle class stays politically quiet and senior advisers privately worry over army leadership.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Memorandum on Tokyo Despatch No. 4000 Regarding Wartime State of Mind in Japan
subfiles.to: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State
